The weights look natural throughout. Head output norms all sit between 0.7 and 1.4 of their layer mean. No MLP neuron is an outlier in gate, up and down at once (the best combined z is about 5, ordinary tail behaviour). So there's no planted or broken component to undo, and the failure is behavioural. Two mechanisms are known so far: markdown mode, which reasons worse, and line-repetition loops, which cause about 26% cut-offs and absorb the mode-switch gain. The copy heads are generic, so the lever has to be the loop-onset decision.

To choose a target I need to know what the loops are about, using the cut answers in gen_1:
- does the gold number appear in the text before the loop starts, so the model had solved the problem and failed to stop;
- is the looped line a restatement of the final result, or something mid-solution?

If most cut answers contain the gold before looping, the repair should strengthen the "conclude with ####" transition. That could convert cut answers directly into correct ones. If the gold usually never appears, loops are a symptom of stuck reasoning, and a stopping fix would only turn cuts into wrong answers.

Loops are a symptom of stuck reasoning, not a failure to stop. Only 11 of 89 looping answers contained the gold number before the loop began, and only 34 of 131 contained it anywhere. Also, the finished answers are only 30% correct. So even a perfect loop breaker would turn most cuts into wrong answers, as the +1.6 mode-switch test hinted. Before choosing a direction I want to rule out cheaper failure modes in the finished answers:
1. Grading or format failures: no "####" marker, or the last number in the text isn't the stated result.
2. Arithmetic slips, where an explicit "a op b = c" equation is wrong.

If many finished-wrong answers contain the gold near the end, or are cut by format, a format-specific fix would pay. If arithmetic slips are frequent, a number-computation component would be the target. If both are rare, the errors are in problem setup, which targeted edits are unlikely to repair, and I'd go back to the mode or loop mechanism.

Two findings. Format is not the issue: only 25 of 265 finished-wrong answers have the gold in their last 200 characters, even though 152 lack the "####" marker. Arithmetic is a real failure: 83 of 366 parsed equations (23%) in finished-wrong answers are wrong, against 30 of 196 (15%) in correct ones. A quarter of the wrong answers (66) contain at least one wrong equation, which contradicts my earlier impression that arithmetic was mostly correct. Some of these may be parser artifacts (percentages, implicit units), so I'll break down the bad equations by operator and operand size and look at a few short examples. If errors concentrate in one operation, for instance multi-digit multiplication or results that need a carry, that narrows the search to a computation-specific mechanism. If they're spread out or mostly parse noise, arithmetic is not a clean target.

Most of the flagged "errors" are parser artifacts. Chained sums like "15 + 10 + 2 = 27" were parsed as "10 + 2 = 27", and repeated "1.50 \times 75 =" chains caused the rest. Real slips exist (21,122 + 3,922 = 24,044) but look rare, and single-step equations of 1 to 4 digits are essentially right. So I'll close arithmetic as a target. That leaves reasoning setup, which is not editable in a targeted way, and the two mechanisms already found: markdown mode and the loop-onset decision.

The onset is a soft choice (first-token logprob of -0.2 to -0.9). I'll look for a residual-stream direction that marks "the next line will duplicate an earlier one" by comparing newline positions just before a duplicated line with newline positions before novel lines in the same texts. Using the same texts controls for the problem and its difficulty. Removing that direction from the outputs of the layers that write it is a hand-built, statistics-based edit.
